projects.title: AI-Assisted Inventory of Speed Management Infrastructure on Washington’s Rural Roads
projects.detail: AI-assisted geospatial inventory of speed-management infrastructure in rural-to-town transition areas and rural community corridors.
projects.context: The immediate task is to establish a usable record of infrastructure before interpreting patterns or selecting locations for later evaluation. My co-PI role connects this inventory work with questions about how the resulting geospatial information can support transportation decisions.

projects.context: The work connects image-based identification with a geospatial representation of walking and cycling facilities. This inventory perspective provides a basis for examining network coverage and gaps in rural settings.

researchStatement: I study how optimization and AI can improve the design, coordination and resilience of operations and supply chain systems.
biography: I study how optimization and artificial intelligence can support decisions in complex operations and supply chains. I am interested in the design of decision models and algorithms, and in how organizations can coordinate resources, adapt to disruption and balance competing objectives.

I am a postdoctoral scholar at the University of Washington, Tacoma Campus, working with Angela Kitali. I received my Ph.D. in Civil Engineering from Florida State University in 2025, advised by Maxim A. Dulebenets. My training spans operations research, engineering data analytics, and harbor, waterway and coastal engineering.
homeResearch: My research connects three questions: how to represent a decision problem mathematically, how to solve it efficiently, and how the resulting decisions should change when data, resources or priorities change. I work with mathematical programming, decomposition, adaptive search and learning, and am interested in their interaction with language models and emerging computing approaches.

The application space is operations and supply chain management: production, distribution, logistics, industrial and service systems, humanitarian operations and public infrastructure. My longer-term interests include integrated planning and control, resilient and sustainable systems, and AI-assisted decision making.
academicContext: My doctoral work examined how hyperheuristics can select and combine search strategies for berth allocation and scheduling, and how those strategies can be hybridized with exact optimization. Subsequent work includes compact mixed-integer formulations and decomposition, learning-guided operator selection, and coordinated truck scheduling at cross-docking facilities.

Alongside this methodological work, I have contributed to sponsored research on humanitarian logistics planning, rail-crossing closure decisions, active-transportation infrastructure and rural speed management. These experiences motivate my broader interest in decision support for connected operations, supply chains and public systems.

At the FAMU–FSU College of Engineering, I taught graduate optimization material as a teaching assistant with delegated instructor responsibilities for Metaheuristics and Hybrid Algorithms, and supported Freight Terminals and Distribution Facilities. My teaching connects mathematical formulation, algorithm design and computational evaluation. I received the college’s Civil and Environmental Engineering Future Faculty Award in 2025.
